explanations.answer: They should never enter the assembly of God
explanations.explanation: That's the rule the people found when the Book of Moses was read aloud: no Ammonite or Moabite should ever enter the assembly of God (Nehemiah 13:1). Notice the word ever. Nehemiah, the governor telling this story, doesn't leave any wiggle room. That one word covers a lot of ground.

explanations.answer: They should be given a share of the land
explanations.explanation: A share of the land sounds generous, friend, but it's not what the people find. The text says no Ammonite or Moabite should ever enter the assembly of God (Nehemiah 13:1). That door stays shut. Besides, my whole land holdings are one cookie planet, so don't ask me about real estate.

explanations.answer: They should serve as guards at the temple
explanations.explanation: Guard duty is a creative guess, baker, but the passage doesn't say it. The Book of Moses says no Ammonite or Moabite should ever enter the assembly of God (Nehemiah 13:1). Ever is the whole rule. I've held some odd jobs in my day, but I never got hired as a guard either.

It's the other way around, friend. The text says they had not met the Israelites with food and water. Instead they hired a man named Balaam to call down a curse against them (Nehemiah 13:2). One cookie and a cup of water at the door would have changed this whole story.

False is right, baker. The text says they had not met the Israelites with food and water. They hired Balaam to call down a curse against them instead (Nehemiah 13:2). Hiring a curse instead of bringing water is a wild way to say hello.

explanations.answer: He turned it into a blessing
explanations.explanation: He turned it into a blessing! Nehemiah says our God had turned the curse into a blessing (Nehemiah 13:2). Balaam was hired to curse, and God changed what the curse became. I've had plans flip on me before, but never in anybody's favor like that.

explanations.answer: He sent it back onto Moab
explanations.explanation: That's not what the text says, friend. It says our God had turned the curse into a blessing (Nehemiah 13:2). Turned, not bounced back. Nothing in the verse mentions it landing on Moab.

explanations.answer: He let it fall on Balaam
explanations.explanation: Balaam was the man hired to do the cursing, so I see why that answer tempts you. But the verse says our God had turned the curse into a blessing (Nehemiah 13:2). It doesn't say the curse fell on anybody. The turning is the whole point.
True! As soon as the people heard this law, they excluded from Israel all of foreign descent (Nehemiah 13:3). No waiting, no sleeping on it. I need three days just to pick a cookie shape.

Not quite, baker. The text says that as soon as the people heard this law, they excluded from Israel all of foreign descent (Nehemiah 13:3). As soon as. I've seen people take longer to answer a group chat.

explanations.answer: Prepares a large room for him
explanations.explanation: Eliashib, the priest in charge of the storerooms, prepares a large room for Tobiah, his relative (Nehemiah 13:4-5). Not a closet, a LARGE room. Family favors can get out of hand fast.

explanations.answer: Gives him a seat with the officials
explanations.explanation: No seat at the table in this verse. Eliashib prepared a large room for Tobiah (Nehemiah 13:5). A seat is one chair, and this was a whole room. Big difference, friend.
Tobiah isn't put over anybody here. The text says Eliashib prepared a large room for him (Nehemiah 13:5). Gatekeepers only show up in that verse as people the stored tithes were prescribed for.

Nope, he wasn't there. Nehemiah says he was not in Jerusalem, because he had returned to Artaxerxes king of Babylon in the thirty-second year of his reign (Nehemiah 13:6). So Eliashib's move happened while Nehemiah was away.

False is right, baker. Nehemiah says that while all this was happening, he was not in Jerusalem, because he had returned to Artaxerxes king of Babylon (Nehemiah 13:6). Step out for a bit and look what happens. I know that feeling.

explanations.answer: He throws all of Tobiah's goods out
explanations.explanation: He threw ALL of Tobiah's household goods out of the room (Nehemiah 13:8). Nehemiah says he was greatly displeased, and that tells you how he took it. The text says all, and all means all. I'd need a bigger mustache to carry that load.

explanations.answer: He lets Tobiah stay if he pays rent
explanations.explanation: Rent? Nehemiah wasn't running a landlord business, friend. The text says he was greatly displeased and threw all of Tobiah's household goods out of the room (Nehemiah 13:8). No lease, no negotiating.

explanations.answer: He moves Tobiah to a smaller room
explanations.explanation: A smaller room is a nice compromise, but the text goes bigger. Nehemiah threw all of Tobiah's household goods out of the room (Nehemiah 13:8). Out, not down the hall.

He ordered that the rooms be purified (Nehemiah 13:9). Tossing out Tobiah's goods was one step, and this was the next order he gave. After the purifying, the articles of the house of God went back in. Clean first, then restock.

explanations.answer: That the rooms be torn down
explanations.explanation: The rooms stay standing, baker. Nehemiah ordered that they be purified, and then the articles of the house of God were restored to them (Nehemiah 13:9). You can't put things back in a pile of rubble.

explanations.answer: That the rooms be locked for good
explanations.explanation: Locked for good would have left those rooms empty. But verse 9 says the articles, the grain offerings and the frankincense went back in. Those rooms get used again, friend.

True. After the purifying, Nehemiah had the articles of the house of God restored to the rooms, along with the grain offerings and frankincense (Nehemiah 13:9). Moving day in reverse, and nobody had to rent a truck.

Not this time, friend. Verse 9 says Nehemiah had the articles of the house of God restored to the rooms, along with the grain offerings and frankincense (Nehemiah 13:9). The purified rooms don't stay empty. Everything back in its place is my favorite kind of ending.

Fields! Nehemiah learns that because the portions for the Levites had not been given to them, all the Levites and singers responsible for the service had gone back to their own fields (Nehemiah 13:10). The service lost its people. I think that's a hard spot to be in.
Not flocks, baker. Verse 10 says the Levites and singers went back to their own fields. Nobody is herding anything in this verse.

Tents sound reasonable, but the text says fields. The Levites and singers went back to their own fields (Nehemiah 13:10). I once lived in a junk drawer for years, so I'm not judging anybody's housing.

explanations.answer: Why has the house of God been neglected
explanations.explanation: Nehemiah asks, “Why has the house of God been neglected?” (Nehemiah 13:11). That's his question for the officials when he rebukes them. After that he gathers the Levites and singers and stations them at their posts. Short question, heavy weight.

explanations.answer: Why has the city wall been left unguarded
explanations.explanation: The wall was a big deal earlier, so I get the mix-up. But here Nehemiah's question is “Why has the house of God been neglected?” (Nehemiah 13:11). His focus is the house of God.

explanations.answer: Why has the Law of Moses not been read
explanations.explanation: The Book of Moses was read aloud back in verse 1, but that's not Nehemiah's question to the officials. He asks, “Why has the house of God been neglected?” (Nehemiah 13:11). He asks it after learning the Levites had gone back to their fields.

Not quite, friend. Nehemiah appoints Shelemiah the priest, Zadok the scribe and Pedaiah of the Levites, with Hanan to assist, because they were considered trustworthy (Nehemiah 13:13). The text says nothing about them being his relatives. Storerooms need people you can count on.

False is right, baker! The text says he picked Shelemiah the priest, Zadok the scribe, Pedaiah of the Levites and Hanan to assist because they were considered trustworthy (Nehemiah 13:13). No relatives are mentioned. I'd trust a team like that with my cookie boxes.

Selling! Nehemiah warns the people against selling food on the Sabbath (Nehemiah 13:15). Treading winepresses, loading donkeys, hauling in grain, wine, grapes and figs. That's a whole operation, and his warning is about the selling.

Cooking isn't in the verse, baker. Nehemiah warns them against selling food on that day (Nehemiah 13:15). The picture is of goods being trodden, loaded and hauled into Jerusalem. Nobody is holding a spatula.

Wasting? Nobody is tossing anything out. They're loading grain onto donkeys and bringing goods in, and Nehemiah warns them against selling food on that day (Nehemiah 13:15). His warning is about the business, friend.
The nobles of Judah. Nehemiah rebukes them and asks, “What is this evil you are doing…” (Nehemiah 13:17). He goes right to the leaders. That's a bold way to start a Sabbath.

The gatekeepers aren't the ones he rebukes here. The text says Nehemiah rebuked the nobles of Judah (Nehemiah 13:17). Later the Levites do get gate duty (Nehemiah 13:22), but that's about guarding, not scolding.
The singers aren't in this scene, friend. Nehemiah rebukes the nobles of Judah (Nehemiah 13:17). The singers showed up earlier, when they'd gone back to their fields (Nehemiah 13:10).

True. Nehemiah says, “And now you are rekindling His wrath against Israel by profaning the Sabbath!” (Nehemiah 13:18). He says it right after asking about their forefathers. I think that was a hard thing for the nobles to hear.

That one is true, baker. Nehemiah tells the nobles, “And now you are rekindling His wrath against Israel by profaning the Sabbath!” (Nehemiah 13:18). Those are his words, and he says them right after asking about their forefathers. It's a stern moment.

explanations.answer: Shut the gates until after the Sabbath
explanations.explanation: Shut the gates! Nehemiah ordered that the gates be shut and not opened until after the Sabbath (Nehemiah 13:19). The evening shadows fall, and the doors close. He also posted some of his servants at the gates. That's closing time with teeth.

explanations.answer: Light a fire beside every gate
explanations.explanation: No fires in the text, friend. When the evening shadows begin to fall, Nehemiah orders the gates shut and not opened until after the Sabbath (Nehemiah 13:19). The shadows are the clock here, not flames.

explanations.answer: Count every load that comes in
explanations.explanation: Counting loads would be handy for a bakery, baker, but that's not his order. He has the gates shut until after the Sabbath, and he posts servants so no load can enter that day (Nehemiah 13:19). If the gates are shut, there's nothing to count.
That's what he says: “…If you do it again, I will lay hands on you.” (Nehemiah 13:21). Short and clear. No long speech needed.
Taking their goods isn't what Nehemiah says, friend. He warns, “…I will lay hands on you.” (Nehemiah 13:21). His words are about the merchants themselves, not their merchandise.
The king doesn't come up in this warning, baker. Nehemiah says, “…I will lay hands on you.” (Nehemiah 13:21). He's talking about doing it himself.

Not quite, friend. The text says, “From that time on, they did not return on the Sabbath.” (Nehemiah 13:21). The merchants had camped outside once or twice, and then they stopped. That's a warning that worked.

False is right, baker. “From that time on, they did not return on the Sabbath.” (Nehemiah 13:21). Once or twice they camped outside, and then the warning did its job. I wish my reminders worked like that. My timer has to go off three times.

Judah! Half of the children spoke the language of Ashdod or of the other peoples, but could not speak the language of Judah (Nehemiah 13:24). Ashdod is the city named back in verse 23. Nehemiah notices what these kids can't speak.

Babylon isn't in this verse, baker. The children speak the language of Ashdod or of other peoples, but they can't speak the language of Judah (Nehemiah 13:24). Babylon came up earlier, as where the king was.
Egypt doesn't show up in this verse, friend. The language these children can't speak is the language of Judah (Nehemiah 13:24). They speak Ashdod's language or that of other peoples.

explanations.answer: No more marrying into those peoples
explanations.explanation: Right, it's about marriage. Nehemiah makes them take an oath before God and says, “You must not give your daughters in marriage to their sons or take their daughters as wives for your sons or for yourselves!” (Nehemiah 13:25). It covers both directions.

explanations.answer: No more trading on the Sabbath
explanations.explanation: Sabbath trading was the earlier problem, handled with the gates and the warning (Nehemiah 13:19-21). This oath is about something else. Different problem, different oath, baker.

The children's languages are part of the scene (Nehemiah 13:24), but the oath isn't about that. Nehemiah says, “You must not give your daughters in marriage…” (Nehemiah 13:25). The promise is about marriages, friend.

Solomon, king of Israel. Nehemiah says there was not a king like him among many nations, and he was loved by his God, yet foreign women drew him into sin (Nehemiah 13:26). If it could happen to a king like that, I think Nehemiah wants the men to take it seriously.
Saul, a king of Israel (1 Samuel 11:15), isn't the one named here. The verse says King Solomon of Israel, a king “loved by his God.” (Nehemiah 13:26). Nice try, baker.
Hezekiah, king of Judah (2 Kings 18:1), isn't named in these verses. Nehemiah names King Solomon of Israel, who was “loved by his God” (Nehemiah 13:26). Close, but Solomon is the one.

Nope, friend. Nehemiah says, “Therefore I drove him away from me.” (Nehemiah 13:28). That's the son of Jehoiada who had become a son-in-law to Sanballat the Horonite. He didn't stay by Nehemiah's side.
False is right, baker. Nehemiah says, “Therefore I drove him away from me.” (Nehemiah 13:28). The son of Jehoiada had become a son-in-law to Sanballat the Horonite, and Nehemiah sent him away.

Defiled the priesthood. Nehemiah prays, “Remember them, O my God, because they have defiled the priesthood and the covenant of the priesthood and of the Levites.” (Nehemiah 13:29). That's how he puts it to God.

Tearing down the wall isn't what he says, friend. His prayer reads, “…because they have defiled the priesthood and the covenant of the priesthood and of the Levites.” (Nehemiah 13:29). The wall isn't mentioned in it.

Mocking the singers isn't in his prayer, baker. Nehemiah says, “…because they have defiled the priesthood and the covenant of the priesthood and of the Levites.” (Nehemiah 13:29). That's the charge he names.
Foreign! Nehemiah says he purified the priests and Levites from everything foreign (Nehemiah 13:30). That's a deep clean, the kind that gets into the corners.
Duties! Nehemiah assigned specific duties to each of the priests and Levites (Nehemiah 13:30). Everybody gets their own job. Even in my bakery, somebody has to know whose job is the oven.
Ancient sounds fitting for priests and Levites, but the text says he purified them from everything foreign (Nehemiah 13:30). That's the word the verse uses, baker.
Robes aren't in this verse, friend. Nehemiah purified the priests and Levites from everything foreign and assigned specific duties to each (Nehemiah 13:30). Nobody is getting new outfits.
Wages aren't what he assigns here. The text says specific duties (Nehemiah 13:30). Pay was the Levites' earlier trouble, when their portions weren't given (Nehemiah 13:10), so I get the pull.
